definition: Request for Comments: a numbered document published by the IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force) that defines an internet standard or best practice. HTTP, OAuth and WebSocket are all specified in RFCs.
example: RFC 9110 defines HTTP methods and status codes; RFC 6749 defines OAuth 2.0.

definition: The Internet Engineering Task Force: the open standards body that develops internet protocols such as HTTP, TLS and OAuth, publishing them as RFCs.
example: The IETF's httpapi working group is drafting standard RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit headers; its Idempotency-Key draft expired without becoming an RFC.

definition: A working document of the IETF. Drafts are not standards: they expire after about six months unless updated, and only some become RFCs.
example: The Idempotency-Key header was proposed in an Internet-Draft that expired without becoming an RFC.

definition: Uniform Resource Identifier: a string that identifies a resource. Every URL is a URI; the term is used in specifications that only need to name something, not necessarily locate it.
example: RFC 9457 error types are URIs such as https://example.com/probs/funds.

definition: The verb at the start of an HTTP request that says what the client wants done to the resource: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS and so on. Each method has defined properties such as safety and idempotency.
example: GET /orders/42 reads order 42; DELETE /orders/42 removes it.

definition: The HTTP method for reading a resource. It is safe (it asks for no state change) and idempotent, so caches, crawlers and retries may repeat it freely.
example: GET /products/5 returns product 5 and changes nothing on the server.

definition: The HTTP method that replaces the target resource's state with the representation in the request. It is idempotent: repeating the same PUT leaves the resource the same.
example: PUT /users/7 with a full user body sets user 7 to exactly that.

definition: The HTTP method for a partial update: the body describes changes rather than a whole replacement. HTTP does not promise PATCH is idempotent; that depends on what the patch does.
example: Setting email to a new value is idempotent; 'add 10 to balance' is not.

definition: The HTTP method that removes a resource. It changes state, so it is not safe, but it is idempotent: deleting twice leaves the resource deleted either way.
example: A second DELETE /orders/42 may return 404, but the server's state is unchanged.

definition: The HTTP method that asks for the same headers a GET would return, but without the body. It is safe and idempotent.
example: A client can send HEAD to check a file's size or ETag without downloading it.

definition: The HTTP method that asks which communication options a resource supports. Browsers send it automatically as the CORS preflight before some cross-origin requests.
example: Before a cross-origin PUT, the browser sends OPTIONS to ask whether PUT is allowed.

definition: An HTTP method that asks the server to echo the request back, for diagnosing proxies. It is safe and idempotent, and is usually disabled in production for security reasons.
An HTTP method that is read-only in intent: the client is not asking for any change of state. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe. Incidental effects such as logging are still allowed.
example: A crawler may follow GET links freely because GET is safe.

definition: The three-digit number at the start of every HTTP response saying how the request went. 2xx means success, 3xx redirect, 4xx a problem with the request, 5xx a problem on the server.
example: 404 means no such resource; 503 means the service is temporarily unavailable.

definition: The HTTP status code for a successful request. What the body contains depends on the method.
The HTTP status code saying the request created a new resource, usually with a Location header pointing at it.
example: POST /orders returns 201 Created and Location: /orders/9831.

definition: The HTTP status code saying the request was accepted for processing but is not finished, and may still fail. It suits long jobs that the client checks on later.
example: POST /reports returns 202 with a link to a job resource the client can poll.

definition: The HTTP status code for success with no response body.
example: A successful DELETE often returns 204.

definition: The HTTP status code a server returns to a conditional GET or HEAD when the client's cached copy is still current, so the body need not be sent again.
example: GET with If-None-Match: "v7" returns 304 if the ETag is still v7.

definition: The HTTP status code saying the request is malformed or invalid, so sending it again unchanged will fail again.
example: A query with an unknown filter name can be rejected with 400.

definition: The HTTP status code meaning the request lacks valid credentials: despite the name it means unauthenticated. It must carry a WWW-Authenticate header saying how to authenticate.
example: An expired access token gets 401, prompting the client to refresh it.

definition: The HTTP status code meaning the server understood the request and refuses it, typically because the authenticated caller lacks permission.
example: A valid token without the admin role gets 403 on an admin endpoint.

definition: The HTTP status code meaning the server has no resource at that URL, or will not reveal that one exists.
The HTTP status code meaning the request clashes with the resource's current state, so it might succeed once that state changes.
example: Signing up with an email that is already registered can return 409.

definition: The HTTP status code returned when a condition in the request headers, such as If-Match, is false, so the server refuses the change.
example: A PUT with If-Match: "v7" gets 412 if the resource is now at v8.

definition: The HTTP status code for a request that is well-formed but semantically invalid, such as an end date before the start date.
The HTTP status code meaning this client has sent too many requests in a given time. Defined in RFC 6585; it usually carries a Retry-After header.
example: Exceeding 100 requests per minute returns 429 with Retry-After: 12.

definition: The generic HTTP status code for an unexpected condition on the server that stopped it fulfilling the request.
The HTTP status code a proxy or gateway returns when the upstream server it called gave an invalid response.
The HTTP status code meaning the server is temporarily unable to handle the request, for example because it is overloaded or in maintenance. It may carry Retry-After.
The HTTP status code a proxy or gateway returns when the upstream server did not answer in time.
Create, read, update, delete: the four basic operations on stored data. In REST they map roughly onto POST, GET, PUT/PATCH and DELETE.
In REST, any named thing a client can act on, such as a customer, an order or a list of orders. Each has its own URL, and clients exchange representations of it, usually JSON.
example: /orders/42 is the resource for order 42.

definition: One URL (often with a particular method) that an API exposes for clients to call.
example: POST /orders/42/cancel is an action endpoint for cancelling order 42.

definition: The content an HTTP message carries after its headers, such as a JSON document.
The HTTP header saying what format the body is in, as a media type such as application/json or text/event-stream.
An HTTP response header giving a URL: the newly created resource after 201, a status resource after 202, or the target of a redirect.
A REST constraint: each request carries everything the server needs to understand it, so the server keeps no client session context between requests. Any server can then handle any request.
example: If server A dies, server B can serve the client's next request because nothing lived only in A.

definition: Handling more load by adding more machines rather than making one machine bigger (vertical scaling). It works best when servers are interchangeable.
example: Going from 3 to 6 identical API servers behind a load balancer roughly doubles capacity.

definition: A load-balancer setting that sends all of one client's requests to the same server, usually because that server holds the client's session in memory.

An HTTP response header holding an opaque version identifier for the current representation of a resource. Clients send it back in If-None-Match (to revalidate a cache) or If-Match (to avoid overwriting someone else's change).
example: ETag: "v7-a1b2"

definition: A request header that makes a write conditional: the server applies it only if the resource's current ETag matches, otherwise it returns 412 Precondition Failed.
example: PUT with If-Match: "v7" fails if another client already moved it to v8.

definition: A request header that makes a GET conditional: if the resource's ETag still matches, the server replies 304 Not Modified instead of resending the body.
An HTTP request whose effect depends on a validator such as an ETag, sent in headers like If-Match or If-None-Match.
Letting clients work without holding locks, then checking at write time that nothing changed meanwhile (for example by comparing a version or ETag) and rejecting the write if it did.
The HTTP header that tells browsers, CDNs and proxies whether and for how long they may cache a response.
example: Cache-Control: max-age=60 allows caching for 60 seconds.

definition: An HTTP response header telling the client how long to wait before trying again, either as a number of seconds or as an HTTP date. Common with 429 and 503.
example: Retry-After: 12 means wait 12 seconds.

definition: The response header a 401 must carry, telling the client which authentication scheme to use and, for bearer tokens, what went wrong.
example: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token"

definition: The HTTP request header that carries the client's credentials, such as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
A token that grants access to whoever presents ('bears') it, with no further proof of identity. That is why stolen bearer tokens are dangerous and why they are kept short-lived.
example: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

aliases: Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State
definition: Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State: the REST constraint that responses include links to the actions a client can take next, so clients navigate the API rather than building URLs themselves.
example: An order response might include a link to cancel it.

definition: Leonard Richardson's grading of web APIs from level 0 (one endpoint, RPC over HTTP) through level 1 (resources) and level 2 (proper HTTP methods and status codes) to level 3 (hypermedia links).
A program that automatically follows links to fetch pages, for example for a search engine or to build link previews. It assumes GET links are safe to follow.
Fetching something before it is asked for, so it is ready if needed. Browsers may prefetch links a user is likely to click.
A server that sits between a client and another server and forwards requests on the client's behalf, often caching, filtering or logging them on the way.
A simple PATCH format (RFC 7396) in which the body is a partial JSON document: listed fields are set to the given values, and null removes a field.
example: {"email": "new@example.com"} changes only the email.

definition: Service level objective: an internal target for a service's reliability or speed, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days.
Service level agreement: a promise to customers about a service's availability or performance, often with penalties if it is missed. In casual use it also means a latency target.
Being the engineer responsible for responding to production alerts out of hours. Alerts that 'page' someone wake them up, so false alarms have a real cost.
One customer organisation sharing a system with others. In a multi-tenant service many customers' data live in the same infrastructure, so every access must check which tenant owns the data.
A popular PHP web framework. It uses the non-standard status code 419 for expired CSRF tokens.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the browser mechanism that lets a page call an API on a different origin only if the API allows it via response headers. For some requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS 'preflight'.
A database mechanism that stops other transactions changing (or sometimes reading) data until the holder finishes, used to make check-and-write steps safe.
The 1997-era text-based version of HTTP, still widely used. One connection carries one request at a time, so clients open several connections in parallel.
The binary version of HTTP (RFC 9113) that multiplexes many concurrent requests as separate streams over one TCP connection and compresses headers.
example: A browser can fetch 50 images over a single HTTP/2 connection at once.

definition: The version of HTTP that runs over QUIC (on UDP) instead of TCP, avoiding TCP's head-of-line blocking between streams.
Carrying several independent streams of data over one shared channel at the same time. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one TCP connection.
When one slow or lost item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it, even items that could otherwise proceed.
Header fields sent after the body of an HTTP message rather than before. gRPC sends its final status (grpc-status) in trailers, which browser JavaScript cannot read reliably.
One message from client to server and the reply coming back. Each round trip costs at least the network round-trip time, so designs try to need fewer of them.
example: At 100 ms per round trip, five sequential calls cost at least half a second.

definition: The fourth generation of mobile network technology. Round-trip times on 4G are typically tens of milliseconds or more, so chatty mobile APIs feel slow.
Receiving more data from an API call than the client needs, wasting bandwidth, parse time and battery.
example: A screen needing a name and avatar gets a 40-field user object.

definition: When one API call does not return enough, so the client has to make further calls to fill the gaps.
A REST convention where the client lists the fields it wants, for example ?fields=id,title, so the server returns only those.
A REST endpoint that returns a resource together with related ones in one response, for example GET /feed?include=author,comments.
The typed description of every object, field and operation a GraphQL API offers. Every query is checked against it.
In GraphQL, the server function that produces the value of one field. A field on a list runs its resolver once per item, which is how the N+1 problem arises.
A performance bug where code runs one query to fetch a list of N items, then one more query per item, giving N+1 queries instead of 2.
example: 20 posts, then one author query each: 21 queries.

definition: A small library from the GraphQL project that collects all the keys requested in one tick of the event loop and loads them with a single batched query, also caching them for the rest of the request.
example: Twenty author lookups become one SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...).

definition: A loop at the heart of runtimes like Node.js that repeatedly takes the next ready event or callback and runs it. One pass is often called a tick.
A GraphQL feature that lets a client ask the server for its own schema, so tools can autocomplete and type-check queries.
An in-browser editor for GraphQL that uses introspection to offer autocomplete, documentation and error checking.
A GraphQL query registered with the server in advance and then called by a short id or hash, which makes requests small, GET-able and cacheable, and can block unregistered queries.
example: GET /graphql?id=9f2c... instead of POSTing the full query text.

definition: A GraphQL operation that changes data, as opposed to a query, which only reads.
A GraphQL operation that keeps a channel open so the server can push results whenever data changes, usually over WebSockets.
A GraphQL server rule that rejects queries nested more deeply than a set number of levels, as a defence against expensive queries.
Estimating how expensive a GraphQL query could be before running it, from its fields and page sizes, and rejecting it if the estimate exceeds a budget.
example: GitHub's GraphQL API charges each query points based on how many nodes it could return.

definition: Google's language-neutral binary serialisation format. You describe messages in a .proto file and generate code that encodes them compactly, identifying each field by number rather than by name.
example: {"sku": "VAN-1", "qty": 150} takes 25 bytes as JSON and 10 as protobuf.

definition: The number given to each field in a protobuf message definition. It, not the field's name, is what goes on the wire, so it must never be reused for a different field.
example: In string sku = 1; the tag is 1.

definition: A small code in each protobuf field key saying how the value is encoded: 0 for varints, 1 and 5 for fixed 64- and 32-bit values, 2 for length-delimited data such as strings.
A variable-length integer encoding: each byte carries 7 bits of the number and one 'more bytes follow' bit, so small numbers take fewer bytes.
example: Values up to 127 take 1 byte; 150 takes 2.

definition: A field in received data that the reader's schema does not know. Protobuf parsers skip or preserve them, which lets old readers cope with new fields.
A protobuf declaration (reserved 3;) that stops a removed field's number or name ever being reused, protecting old readers from misreading new data.
Protobuf's zigzag-encoded signed integer types. Plain int32 and int64 fields always spend 10 bytes on a negative value, while sint32 and sint64 keep small negative numbers small.

A way to write arbitrary bytes as text using 64 printable characters; every 3 bytes become 4 characters. base64url swaps two characters so the result is safe in URLs. It is an encoding, not encryption: anyone can decode it.
example: A 256-byte RSA signature becomes 342 base64url characters.

definition: Producing source code automatically from a definition such as a .proto file or an OpenAPI document, so clients and servers share an exact contract.
In RPC, generated code that makes a remote call look like a local function call: the client stub serialises the arguments and sends them, and the server stub decodes them and calls your handler.
A standard machine-readable format for describing REST APIs: their endpoints, parameters and response shapes. Tools generate documentation and client code from it.
The simplest gRPC call style: one request, one response.
A gRPC call style where the client sends one request and the server replies with a stream of messages.
A gRPC call style where the client sends a stream of messages and the server replies once.
A gRPC call style where client and server both send streams of messages independently over one call.

In gRPC, the absolute time by which a call must finish. With deadline propagation, downstream calls inherit the remaining time, and when it runs out the call fails with DEADLINE_EXCEEDED so every hop can stop work.
example: A 500 ms deadline set at checkout leaves 430 ms for a call made two hops later.

definition: A variant of gRPC that browsers can use: it moves the status out of HTTP trailers into the body. A proxy such as Envoy usually translates it to native gRPC. It supports unary and server-streaming calls only.
An RPC protocol from Buf that works with protobuf definitions and is callable from browsers with plain HTTP, while remaining compatible with gRPC and gRPC-Web servers.
An open-source L7 proxy, originally from Lyft, widely used as an edge gateway, a service-mesh sidecar and a gRPC-Web translator.
A command-line tool for making HTTP (and other) requests, used everywhere for testing and debugging APIs.
example: curl -X POST https://api.example.com/orders

definition: A command-line tool like curl for calling gRPC services, using server reflection or .proto files to encode requests.
A gRPC service that describes the server's own services and messages at runtime, so tools such as grpcurl can call it without the .proto files.
Load balancing at the transport layer (layer 4 of the OSI model): the balancer picks a backend per TCP connection, without looking at individual HTTP requests.
Load balancing at the application layer (layer 7): the balancer understands HTTP and can route and spread individual requests, not just connections.
The client itself learns all backend addresses and spreads its calls across them, instead of going through a central load balancer.
A server setting that closes long-lived connections after a set time, so clients reconnect and load spreads across new or less busy servers.
Short for load balancer: the component that spreads incoming traffic across several servers.
Using several programming languages in one system, for example services written in Go, Java and Python that must all talk to each other.
A set of open connections a client keeps and reuses, rather than opening a new connection for every request.
Measurements such as metrics and events that devices or services send automatically for monitoring.
Foreign exchange: converting between currencies. An FX service supplies exchange rates.
Queries per second: how many requests a service handles each second.
A measure of load: how many requests arrive or are served each second.
example: 1 million clients polling every 5 s generate 200,000 req/s.

definition: Returning a long list in pieces (pages) of bounded size, with a way for the client to ask for the next piece. It keeps every request's cost predictable.
example: Stripe's list APIs return 10 items by default and at most 100.

definition: Paging by telling the server how many rows to skip (offset) and how many to return (limit). Simple, but deep pages are slow because skipped rows are still walked, and pages shift when rows are inserted or deleted.
example: GET /orders?limit=20&offset=40 returns rows 41 to 60.

definition: Paging by asking for rows after the last one seen, using its sort key (for example created_at and id) in a WHERE clause. With an index, every page costs about the same however deep it is.
example: WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 21

definition: A token the server returns with a page that tells it where the next page starts. It should be opaque: clients pass it back without reading or building it.
An extra, unique sort column (usually the id) added so that rows with equal values in the main sort key still have one fixed order.
example: Sorting by (created_at, id) gives a total order even when timestamps are equal.

definition: Using an index's tree structure to jump straight to a starting key, rather than reading through entries one by one.
The number of child pointers one B-tree index page holds. It is often a few hundred, so even a table of millions of rows is only a few levels deep and a seek reads only a few pages.
example: With a fan-out of 300, three levels reach 300 × 300 × 300 = 27 million entries.

definition: The SQL aggregate that counts rows. An exact count over many matching rows can be slow because the database must visit each one.
The step-by-step strategy a database chooses to run a SQL query, such as which index to use. The planner also keeps statistics that can give approximate row counts cheaply.
The SQL statement that reads rows from tables.
example: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 42;

definition: The SQL statement that adds new rows to a table.
The SQL statement that changes values in existing rows.
example: UPDATE orders SET paid = true WHERE id = 42;

definition: A PostgreSQL clause on INSERT that says what to do when the new row would break a unique constraint: do nothing, or update the existing row (an upsert).
An explicit list of what is permitted, with everything else rejected. Safer than trying to list everything that is forbidden.
example: Only status and created_after may be used as filters; anything else gets 400.

definition: A name=value pair after the ? in a URL, used for filters, sorting and paging.
example: In /orders?status=open&limit=50 there are two query parameters.

definition: RFC 9457's standard JSON format for API errors, with fields such as type (a stable URI for the error class), title, status, detail and instance.
A unique identifier attached to each request and written into every log line about it, so support staff can find exactly what happened.
The list of function calls active when an error happened. Useful for developers, but leaking it to API clients reveals internals.
Keeping old and new behaviours of an API available side by side, selected by a version in the URL (/v2/orders), a header or a date, so breaking changes don't break existing clients.
example: Stripe pins each account to a dated version such as 2024-06-20.

definition: A change to an API that makes some existing, correctly written clients fail, such as removing or renaming a field or making an optional field required.
The property that a new version still works with clients and data built for older versions.
example: Adding a new optional field is backwards-compatible; renaming one is not.

definition: "Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others" (Jon Postel). For APIs it means clients should ignore fields they don't recognise, so servers can add fields safely.
A type whose value must be one of a fixed list of names, such as PAID or REFUNDED. Clients that assume the list never grows can crash when a new value appears.
Turning bytes such as JSON text back into objects in memory: the reverse of serialisation. Strict deserialisers reject unknown fields, which turns additive API changes into failures.

"With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody." Anything clients can see becomes an unofficial contract.
Marking a feature as on its way out: still working for now, but scheduled for removal, so users should migrate.
An HTTP response header (RFC 9745) saying that the resource is or will be deprecated, so client tooling can warn developers.
An HTTP response header (RFC 8594) giving the date after which a resource is expected to stop responding.
example: Sunset: Sat, 31 Oct 2026 23:59:59 GMT

definition: Deliberately making a deprecated API fail for short, announced windows before its removal, so forgotten integrations show up while there is still time to fix them.
A dated list of the changes in each release of a product or API.
Software development kit: a library (and often tools) that makes an API easy to call from a particular language.
example: Stripe's Python SDK handles retries and idempotency keys for you.

definition: An API's documented promise about what repeating a request does, including the key's scope, how long keys are kept and what happens when a key is reused with different parameters.
A delivery guarantee where each message is sent once and never retried: nothing is duplicated, but some messages can be lost.
In Amazon SQS, how long a received message stays hidden from other consumers. If the consumer doesn't delete it in time, it becomes visible and is delivered again.
A Kafka producer setting that tags messages with sequence numbers so the broker drops duplicates caused by the producer's own retries, within one partition and producer session.
How strictly a database keeps concurrent transactions from seeing each other's effects. Under Read Committed, the PostgreSQL default, two transactions can both read 'absent' before either inserts.
In Brandur Leach's idempotency design, one step of a multi-step operation that runs inside a single database transaction, followed by a recorded recovery point.
A saved marker of how far a multi-step operation got, so a retry can resume from there instead of starting over.
The payment system (such as Visa or Mastercard) that carries card authorisations and charges between merchants' and cardholders' banks.
In retries and reconnects, a random amount of variation in the wait time, so clients that failed together try again at different moments instead of in one synchronised wave.
example: Without jitter, 10,000 clients that failed at the same instant all retry 1.6 s later; with full jitter they spread over the whole 1.6 s.

definition: AWS's jitter strategy for retries: wait a uniformly random time between zero and the capped exponential backoff value, so clients that failed together spread their retries out evenly.
example: 10,000 clients with full jitter over 2 s retry at about 5,000 per second instead of all at once.

definition: A helper process deployed next to each service instance, often a proxy such as Envoy, that handles networking concerns like retries, TLS and metrics.
A random choice in which every value in a range is equally likely. Its average is the midpoint of the range.
example: A wait drawn uniformly from 0 to 1.6 s averages 0.8 s.

definition: A cap on how many requests a client may make in a period, such as 100 per minute. The component that enforces it is a rate limiter.
The amount of use a client is allowed in a period, such as 5,000 requests per hour on a paid plan.
One tenant on shared infrastructure using so much capacity that other tenants' performance suffers.
An attack that tries large lists of usernames and passwords leaked from other sites against a login, betting that people reuse passwords. Login rate limits slow it down.
Automatically downloading large amounts of data from a website or API, often against the owner's wishes.
Trying many values in turn, such as ids or usernames, to discover which exist or to read data that isn't yours.
example: Requesting /invoices/1000, /invoices/1001, ... to find other customers' invoices.

definition: Running a trained machine-learning model to produce an output, such as generating text. It is computationally expensive, so it is often rate limited.
Artificial intelligence: software that performs tasks such as understanding or generating language that normally need human intelligence.
HTTP response headers that tell a client its quota, how much is left and when it resets. An IETF draft defines RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit; many APIs use older X-RateLimit-* headers.
example: RateLimit-Policy: "min";q=100;w=60

definition: A time written as the number of seconds since 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970.
example: 1767225600 is midnight UTC on 1 January 2026.

definition: A rate-limiting algorithm: each client has a bucket holding up to a set capacity of tokens, refilled at a steady rate; each request spends one token and is rejected if none are left. It allows bursts up to the capacity and averages out at the refill rate.
example: Capacity 10, refill 2 per second: 10 requests at once, then 2 per second.

definition: How fast a token bucket gains tokens, in tokens per second. It sets the long-run average request rate.
The most tokens a token bucket can hold. It sets the largest burst of requests allowed at once.
A short spike of many requests arriving close together, well above the average rate.

A rate-limiting and traffic-shaping algorithm: requests join a fixed-size queue that is drained at a constant rate, and new requests are dropped when the queue is full. The output is smooth but requests wait.

A rate-limiting algorithm that counts each client's requests in fixed clock periods, such as each calendar minute, and resets the count at each boundary. Cheap, but a client can get up to twice the limit across a boundary.
The flaw in fixed-window rate limiting: a client can use the whole limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, getting double the rate over a short span.
A rate-limiting algorithm that stores the timestamp of every request and counts those inside the last window. Exact, but memory grows with traffic.
A rate-limiting approximation that keeps counts for the current and previous fixed windows and weights the previous count by how much of it the sliding window still covers.
example: 80 last minute, 30 this minute, 15 s in: 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90.

definition: Delaying traffic so that it leaves at a controlled rate, rather than rejecting it, to protect a downstream system.
A widely used web server and reverse proxy. Its limit_req module rate-limits requests with a leaky bucket whose queue size is the burst parameter.
The Redis command that adds 1 to a counter and returns the new value, atomically.
The Redis command that sets a time to live on a key, after which Redis deletes it.
A Redis data type holding unique members each with a numeric score, kept in score order. ZADD adds a member, ZCARD counts them, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE removes a score range.
example: Use request timestamps as scores to build a sliding window log.

definition: A Redis data type that stores field-value pairs under one key. HSET writes fields, HGET reads one, HMGET reads several.

Redis transaction commands: MULTI queues commands and EXEC runs them together without interleaving. WATCH aborts EXEC if a watched key changed, for optimistic retries. Queued commands cannot branch on earlier results.
Redis's built-in sharding mode, which spreads keys across several primary nodes by hash slot.
A data store, such as Redis or a database, that every server in a fleet reads and writes, so they share state such as rate-limit counters or sessions.
Allowing requests through when a protective check (such as the rate limiter's store) is unavailable, choosing availability over enforcement.
Rejecting requests when a protective check is unavailable, choosing safety over availability. Sensible for security limits such as login attempts.
A single key that receives a disproportionate share of traffic, overloading the one shard that holds it.
The latency of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile (p99), which matters more to users than the average.
The point where outside traffic first enters your system, such as a CDN, API gateway or edge proxy. Checks done there stop bad requests before they cost anything further in.
Web application firewall: a filter in front of web apps and APIs that blocks malicious requests using rules, such as known attack patterns or rate limits.
A large CDN and network security company whose edge network offers caching, DDoS protection, WAF and rate limiting.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's cloud computing platform, offering services such as SQS, API Gateway and load balancers.
Microsoft's code-hosting platform. Its public REST and GraphQL APIs and its webhooks are common examples in API design.
AWS's managed API gateway service, offering REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs, with token-bucket throttling (rate and burst).
Short for authentication: establishing who the caller is.
Short for authorisation: deciding whether an identified caller may do what it is asking.
The Open Worldwide Application Security Project, a non-profit that publishes security guidance such as the OWASP Top 10 lists of the most critical web and API risks.

An API flaw where the server checks that the caller is logged in but not that the specific object requested belongs to them, so changing an id in the URL exposes someone else's data. It tops the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023).
example: GET /invoices/1009 returns another company's invoice to any logged-in user.

definition: Server-side state that remembers a logged-in user between requests. The browser holds only a random session id, usually in a cookie, which the server looks up.
Where a server keeps session records, such as Redis or a database, so that any server in the fleet can look a session up.
A small piece of data a server asks the browser to store (with Set-Cookie) and send back automatically on later requests to the same site.
example: Set-Cookie: sid=9f8c...; HttpOnly; Secure

definition: A cookie attribute that stops page JavaScript reading the cookie, so an XSS bug cannot steal it. The browser still sends it with requests.
A cookie attribute controlling whether the browser sends the cookie on requests that come from other sites; Lax and Strict values help block CSRF.
Cancelling a credential before it would naturally expire, so it stops working.
example: Deleting a session record revokes that session at once; a self-contained JWT keeps working until it expires unless you add a deny-list.

definition: The fields in a JWT payload. Registered claims include sub (subject: who the token is about), iss (issuer), aud (audience: which service it is for), exp (expiry time), nbf (not valid before) and jti (unique token id). Verifiers must check the ones their profile requires.
example: {"sub":"user_42","aud":"orders-api","exp":1767225600}

definition: The header field naming the algorithm used to sign a JWT, such as RS256. Verifiers must not trust it: they should pin the algorithms they accept, or attackers can send alg: none or switch to HS256.

JWT header fields that hint which key verifies the token: kid names a key id; jku and x5u give URLs to fetch keys from. Look kid up only in your own trusted key set, and never fetch keys from a URL the token supplies.
JSON Web Signature (RFC 7515): the signed form of a JWT, three base64url parts header.payload.signature. It proves integrity, not secrecy.
JSON Web Encryption (RFC 7516): the encrypted form of a JWT, used when the claims themselves must be kept secret.
JSON Web Key Set: a JSON document, usually published at a URL, listing an issuer's public keys so verifiers can check its tokens.
The JWT algorithm HMAC with SHA-256: one shared secret both signs and verifies, so every verifier could also forge tokens.
The JWT algorithm RSA signature with SHA-256: the issuer signs with a private key and anyone with the public key can verify but not sign.
The JWT algorithm ECDSA on the P-256 curve with SHA-256: an asymmetric signature like RS256 but with much smaller keys and signatures.
Cryptography using a key pair: a private key that only the owner holds and a public key anyone can have. Signatures made with the private key are checked with the public one.
A text format for keys and certificates: base64 data between lines such as -----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----.
A JWT attack in which a verifier expecting RS256 is tricked by an HS256 header into using the RSA public key as an HMAC secret. Since the public key is public, the attacker can forge valid tokens.
A browser API that stores key-value data for a site. Any script running on the page can read it, so a single XSS bug can steal tokens kept there.
A credential an OAuth client sends to an API (usually as a bearer token) to access resources within the granted scopes. It should be short-lived, typically minutes.
A longer-lived OAuth credential the client exchanges at the authorisation server for new access tokens, giving the server a chance to re-check the account each time.
Issuing a new refresh token every time one is used and invalidating the old one. If an old one is presented again, the server can treat it as theft and revoke the whole family.
A list of things to reject, such as revoked token ids (jti values) kept until those tokens expire.
Letting an app act on your behalf on another service, with limited permissions, without giving it your password. This is what OAuth provides.
A named permission that limits what an access token can do, such as gmail.readonly or orders:read.
In OAuth, the user who owns the data and grants an app access to it.
In OAuth, the API that holds the protected data and accepts access tokens.
In OAuth, the server that logs the user in, asks for consent and issues access and refresh tokens.
In OAuth, the application that wants to access a user's data on their behalf, such as a budgeting app.
An OAuth client that cannot keep a secret, such as a mobile or single-page app whose code users can inspect.
An OAuth client that can keep a client secret safe because it runs on a server, such as a traditional server-rendered web app.
A password-like value a confidential OAuth client uses to authenticate itself to the authorisation server.
One of OAuth's defined ways for a client to obtain an access token, such as the authorisation code, client credentials or device code grant.
The OAuth flow for apps with a user: the browser is redirected to log in, comes back with a short-lived code, and the client exchanges that code (with PKCE) at the token endpoint for tokens.

Proof Key for Code Exchange (RFC 7636, pronounced 'pixy'): the client sends a hash of a secret random verifier at the start of the OAuth flow and the verifier itself when redeeming the code, so a stolen code is useless to anyone else.
In PKCE, the high-entropy random string (43 to 128 characters) the client keeps secret and sends only to the token endpoint.
In PKCE, the value derived from the code verifier (with S256, its SHA-256 hash in base64url) that the client sends in the authorisation request.
The PKCE challenge method in which the challenge is BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)). The alternative plain method sends the verifier itself and gives up most of the protection.
An OAuth attack in which an attacker plants a stolen authorisation code into a legitimate client's callback so the client redeems it and logs the attacker in as the victim. PKCE stops it.
The address the authorisation server sends the browser back to, carrying the code. It must exactly match a registered value so codes cannot be sent to an attacker's URL.
Communication that passes through the user's browser, such as redirects, where it can leak into history, logs or other apps. The back channel is a direct server-to-server request.
The authorisation server URL where a client exchanges a code, refresh token or client credentials for tokens, in a direct request rather than through the browser.
The authorisation server URL the browser is redirected to so the user can log in and consent.
The OAuth grant for machine-to-machine calls with no user: a service authenticates as itself (client id and secret, a signed JWT or mTLS) and receives a token.
The OAuth grant for devices without a usable browser, such as TVs and CLIs: the device shows a code and you approve it on your phone.
A deprecated OAuth grant that returned the access token directly in the redirect URL fragment, exposing it to browser history and scripts. RFC 9700 says not to use it; OAuth 2.1 removes it.
A deprecated OAuth grant in which the client collects the user's password and sends it to the authorisation server. RFC 9700 says it must not be used.
An IETF draft (still not an RFC in October 2026) consolidating OAuth 2.0 and its security best practices: PKCE for the code flow, exact redirect matching, and no implicit or password grants.
An identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: as well as an access token, the client gets an ID token saying who the user is. 'Sign in with Google' uses it.
In OpenID Connect, a signed JWT telling the client app who logged in. Its audience is the client, so it must not be sent to an API as an access token.
An OpenID Connect endpoint that returns claims about the logged-in user when called with an access token.
A JSON document an OpenID provider publishes listing its endpoints, keys and supported features.
Multi-factor authentication: requiring two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus a code from a phone.
Logging in to one service with an identity from another, such as 'Sign in with Google'.
Single-page application: a web app that loads once and then updates the page with JavaScript, calling APIs directly from the browser.
Command-line interface: a program you use by typing commands in a terminal.
A long random secret that identifies and authenticates a calling project or account. Store only a hash of it, scope it, and allow several per account so it can be rotated.
example: Stripe secret keys start sk_live_ so leaked ones are easy to recognise.

definition: Automatically searching code repositories for leaked credentials such as API keys, using recognisable prefixes and patterns.
Replacing a key or secret with a new one on a schedule or after a suspected leak, usually with an overlap period in which both are accepted.
Mutual TLS: TLS in which the client also presents a certificate, so both sides prove their identity at the transport layer.
A signed document (normally X.509) binding a public key to an identity, issued by a certificate authority. TLS uses it to prove who is at the other end.
An access token tied to the client's TLS certificate (RFC 8705), so it only works over a connection where that certificate's private key is proven.
Demonstrating Proof of Possession (RFC 9449): the client signs a small proof with its own private key on every request, binding its access token to that key at the application layer.
A token that only works when presented by the client it was issued to, because using it requires proving possession of a key (via mTLS or DPoP).
Infrastructure, usually sidecar proxies plus a control plane, that handles service-to-service networking such as mTLS, retries and metrics without changing application code.
An open-source service mesh that uses Envoy sidecars and issues each workload a short-lived certificate for mTLS.
An open-source service mesh with its own lightweight proxy, providing automatic mTLS, retries and load balancing.

aliases: Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone
definition: Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone: a standard for giving each workload a verifiable identity (a SPIFFE ID in a certificate).
Regulated schemes that let licensed third parties access bank account data and payments through APIs, with strong client authentication such as mTLS.
Role-based access control: users get roles, and roles carry permissions. Simple to audit, but strains when rules depend on context.
example: alice -> editor; editor -> posts:read, posts:write

definition: Attribute-based access control: decisions are policies over attributes of the user, resource, action and environment, such as 'same department and not locked'.
Relationship-based access control: permissions follow relationships in a graph, such as membership of a group that can view a folder containing a document.
The RBAC failure mode where context-dependent rules force ever more specific roles, such as editor-uk and editor-uk-weekend.
An open-source policy engine that evaluates authorisation rules written in its Rego language against JSON input.
Open Policy Agent's declarative language for writing policies.
AWS Identity and Access Management: controls who can do what in an AWS account using JSON policies that can test attributes and conditions.
Google's global authorisation system, described in a 2019 paper, storing relationships as tuples and answering 'can this user see this object?' for products such as Drive and YouTube.
In Zanzibar-style systems, a stored fact of the form object#relation@user, such as doc:spec#viewer@group:eng.
An open-source relationship-based authorisation system inspired by Zanzibar.
An open-source database for relationship-based permissions, inspired by Zanzibar.
The fixed-size output of a cryptographic hash function such as SHA-256, used as a fingerprint of the input: it is infeasible to find a different input with the same digest.
In security, a measure of how unpredictable a secret is, in bits. A high-entropy value cannot be guessed by trying candidates.
A function that is easy to compute but infeasible to reverse, such as a cryptographic hash.
User interface: the screens and controls people use to interact with software.
Asking the server for updates repeatedly on a fixed timer. Simple, but most responses are empty and an update waits on average half the interval.
example: Polling every 5 s gives about 2.5 s average delay.

definition: The client asks for updates and the server holds the request open until there is data or a timeout (often 20 to 60 s), then the client immediately asks again. Updates arrive almost at once over plain HTTP.
The server sending data to the client as soon as it changes, rather than waiting to be asked. Long polling, SSE and WebSockets are ways to do it.
A standard for the server to stream text events to a browser over one long-lived HTTP response. The browser's EventSource API reconnects automatically and resumes with Last-Event-ID. One-way only.
The browser API that opens a Server-Sent Events stream, delivers each event to your code and reconnects automatically if the connection drops.
The header an EventSource sends when it reconnects, carrying the id of the last event it received so the server can replay anything missed.
A short store of recent events kept so that reconnecting clients can be sent what they missed.
Communication where both sides can send at the same time, independently. WebSockets are full-duplex; SSE is one-way.
The unit of data on a WebSocket connection: a 2 to 14 byte header (opcode, length, mask) followed by the payload. Messages may span several frames.
The opening exchange that sets up a connection or protocol, such as the WebSocket HTTP upgrade or the TLS handshake.
An HTTP/1.1 mechanism for switching a connection to another protocol. The client sends Upgrade: websocket and the server agrees with 101 Switching Protocols.
Handshake headers in which the client sends a random key and the server returns a hash derived from it, proving it understood the WebSocket upgrade.
The URL schemes for WebSockets: ws:// is plain, wss:// runs over TLS like https://.
A connection kept open for many messages over minutes or hours, rather than opened per request. It ties each client to one server.
Holding state that later requests depend on. A stateful server cannot simply be swapped for another without losing that state.
With event-driven (non-blocking) I/O one thread handles many connections by reacting to readiness events instead of dedicating a blocked thread to each.

Memory the operating system's kernel keeps for each network socket (the program's handle on a connection) to hold data waiting to be sent or read. Every open connection uses some, which is one reason idle connections still cost memory.
A number the operating system gives a process for each open file or socket. Systems cap how many a process may hold (ulimit -n), which limits connections.
A temporary port number the OS assigns to the client side of an outgoing connection. A proxy opening many connections to one backend can run out of them.
A server tier that holds clients' persistent WebSocket connections and passes messages between them and the backend services.
A lookup, often in Redis, recording which gateway server each user or connection is attached to, so messages can be routed there.
How long a load balancer, proxy or NAT device keeps a connection open with no traffic before closing it.
example: AWS Application Load Balancers default to 60 s.

definition: AWS's L7 load balancer for HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC and WebSocket traffic.
A load-balancing rule that sends each new connection to the server with the fewest active ones.
Huge numbers of clients reconnecting at once, for example after a server restart, overloading authentication and the remaining servers.
Taking a server out of service gently: stop accepting new connections, then close existing ones gradually.
A counter attached to each message in order, so a receiver can detect gaps and ask for just what it missed.
A JavaScript library for real-time messaging over WebSockets (with fallbacks), adding rooms, acknowledgements and automatic reconnection. Its Redis adapter broadcasts between server nodes.
The real-time messaging layer of the Elixir Phoenix web framework.
A managed real-time messaging service that holds client connections for you.
A managed real-time messaging service for pushing events to browsers and apps.
Microsoft Azure's managed service for WebSocket connections and publish/subscribe messaging.
Large language model: an AI model trained on vast text that generates text token by token. APIs often stream its output over SSE.
A model of events arriving at random, independently, at a constant average rate. The gaps between events then follow an exponential distribution.
Running a system under realistic or extreme simulated traffic to measure its real capacity and find what breaks first.
A keyed hash (usually HMAC-SHA256) of a webhook's timestamp and raw body, sent in a header so the receiver can check the event really came from the provider and was not altered.
A secret value known to both sender and receiver and to nobody else, used to compute and check signatures such as webhook HMACs.
Comparing two secrets in a way that always takes the same time, whatever the inputs, so an attacker cannot learn how many leading characters matched.
example: Python's hmac.compare_digest and Node's crypto.timingSafeEqual do this.

definition: Learning secret information by measuring how long operations take, for example a comparison that stops at the first mismatching byte.
An open specification for webhook delivery that standardises the webhook-id, webhook-timestamp and webhook-signature headers and signs id.timestamp.body.
Capturing a genuine, validly signed message and sending it again later. A signature alone does not stop it; a signed timestamp or deduplication does.
GitHub webhook headers: X-Hub-Signature-256 carries an HMAC-SHA256 of the body only (no timestamp); X-GitHub-Delivery is a delivery id that is not covered by the signature.
The unique identifier a provider gives each webhook event, used by receivers to deduplicate repeated deliveries.
Accepting work, acknowledging it immediately and doing it later in the background, so the caller doesn't wait.
A fixed set of processes or threads that take jobs from a queue and run them. If slow jobs occupy every worker, everything else waits.
A queueing rule: the average number of items in a system equals their arrival rate times the average time each spends there.
example: 10 deliveries per second each taking 25 s keep 250 workers busy.

definition: Keeping customers' workloads separate (separate queues, concurrency limits) so one customer's slow or failing endpoint can't starve the others.
A provider endpoint listing recent events, so consumers can reconcile anything their webhook endpoint missed.
Comparing your records with an authoritative source and fixing any differences, for example after missed webhooks or an unknown payment outcome.
Messages arriving in a different order from the one in which they were created, for example because of retries or parallel delivery.
An event whose payload holds little more than an id, telling the receiver to fetch the object's current state rather than trusting a possibly stale snapshot.
Applying an update only if its version is newer than the stored one, so a late, stale event can't overwrite newer data.
example: UPDATE subs SET plan=$p, ver=$v WHERE id=$id AND ver < $v

definition: Delivering events for the same object strictly in order (one in flight at a time per key) while different objects proceed in parallel.
A reverse proxy in front of many services that handles cross-cutting concerns in one place: routing, authentication, rate limits, TLS termination and logging.
A need shared by many parts of a system, such as authentication, logging or rate limiting, best handled once rather than in every service.
Decrypting TLS at a proxy or gateway so the services behind it receive plain requests (or a new internal connection).
How well you can understand a system's internal state from what it emits: logs, metrics and traces.
A log with one line per request: time, client, method, path, status and duration.
Following one request across many services by passing a trace id in headers and recording each hop's timing.
Sending a small share of traffic to a new version first, and widening it only if nothing goes wrong.
An open-source API gateway built on NGINX.
Google Cloud's managed API management and gateway platform.
Microsoft Azure's managed API gateway and developer-portal service.
One large application containing all of a system's functionality, deployed as a single unit, so every team's change goes through it.
A thin backend built for one kind of client (iOS, web) and owned by that frontend's team. It aggregates and trims core-service responses into exactly what its screens need.
A BFF that runs the OAuth flow server-side and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie, so tokens never reach JavaScript.
Directions in a chain of calls: downstream services are the ones you call, upstream ones call you (proxies also call the server they forward to 'upstream').
All the servers running one service.
Portable Document Format: a file format for documents that look the same everywhere.
The 2022 IETF standard defining HTTP's semantics: methods and their safety and idempotency, status codes and common headers.
The 2012 IETF standard defining the OAuth 2.0 authorisation framework.
The 2015 IETF standard defining PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) for OAuth.
The 2015 IETF standard defining JSON Web Token (JWT).
The 2020 IETF best-current-practice document on using JWTs safely: pin algorithms, validate claims, avoid trusting key hints.
The January 2025 IETF best-current-practice document for OAuth 2.0 security: PKCE, exact redirect matching, no implicit or password grants, and refresh token protection.
The 2011 IETF standard defining the WebSocket protocol.
The 2023 IETF standard defining Problem Details, a JSON format for HTTP API errors. It replaced RFC 7807.
The 2012 IETF standard that added extra HTTP status codes, including 429 Too Many Requests.
The IETF standard for using OAuth bearer tokens in HTTP requests, including the Authorization: Bearer header and WWW-Authenticate error codes.
The IETF standard for OAuth mutual-TLS client authentication and certificate-bound access tokens.
The IETF standard defining DPoP, proof-of-possession for OAuth tokens at the application layer.
The IETF standard for running WebSockets over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection.

Calls made by one backend service to another with no user directly involved, such as Orders calling Payments. They are authenticated with service identities such as client credentials or mTLS rather than user logins.

An HTTP request header carrying a unique client-generated key, so the server can recognise a retried POST and return the first result instead of acting twice. Stripe and others use it; the IETF draft that would have standardised it expired without becoming an RFC.
example: Idempotency-Key: 8e03978e-40d5-43e8-bc93-6894a57f9324

definition: HMAC (a keyed-hash message authentication code) built on the SHA-256 hash. Only someone holding the secret key can produce the 32-byte result for a given message, so it proves the message came from a key holder and was not altered.
example: Stripe signs each webhook with HMAC-SHA256 over the timestamp, a dot and the raw body, and sends it as 64 hex characters.

definition: WebSocket control frames: one side sends a ping and the other must answer with a pong. Sent every few tens of seconds as a heartbeat, they keep idle connections from being closed by load balancers and reveal dead peers.
Microsoft's cloud computing platform, offering managed services such as Azure API Management and Azure Web PubSub.
